Rescission is the act of officially canceling, wiping out, or undoing an agreement, contract, or law — in such a way that it is treated as though it never existed in the first place.

That phrase — "never existed in the first place" — is the absolute heart of this word. Rescission doesn't simply end something and move on. It erases the thing going backward in time, restoring everyone involved to the exact position they were in before the agreement ever happened.
The Big Idea: Turning Back the Clock

Think of it this way. Imagine you and a friend make a deal. You give him your bike, and he gives you $200. Later, you discover he lied to you to make the deal happen. A regular cancellation would say, "The deal is over — you keep your money and I keep my bike." But rescission goes further and says: "This deal is being erased. It never legally happened. Give me my bike back, and I'll give you your $200 back. We are back to square one."

This "return to square one" quality is what makes rescission different from almost every other word that involves ending or canceling something. It is retroactive — meaning it acts backward, not just forward.
Where Rescission Is Used

Rescission is most commonly used in three areas:

1. Contract Law (the most common use)

In everyday legal life, rescission is used to completely undo a contract. When a contract is rescinded, it is voided from the very beginning — lawyers call this void ab initio, meaning "void from the start." Any goods exchanged must be returned, any money paid must be refunded, and any work done may need to be compensated, so that no one is left worse off than before the contract existed.

2. Real Estate

Rescission is especially important in property transactions. In many countries, when you sign a contract to buy a home, you are legally given a short window of time — often called a "rescission period" or "cooling-off period" — during which you can change your mind, cancel the purchase contract, and get your deposit back. The contract is treated as though it was never signed. This protects buyers from making rushed decisions on one of the biggest purchases of their lives.

3. Laws and Government Orders

Rescission is also used when a government, court, or authority formally cancels a law, regulation, order, or decision. For example, a government might pass a rescission of a previous policy, meaning that policy is officially withdrawn and no longer has any force — as if it were struck off the books.
Why Would Rescission Happen? (The Grounds)

A contract or agreement is not rescinded randomly. There must be a valid legal reason. The most recognized reasons include:

Fraud — One party deliberately lied or deceived the other to get them to sign. If you buy a car and the seller secretly knew the engine was broken and lied about it, that is fraud, and you may be entitled to rescission.

Misrepresentation — Similar to fraud, but the false statement may have been made without intent to deceive. Even an honest but incorrect statement that caused you to enter a contract can be grounds for rescission.

Mistake — Both parties were operating under a fundamental misunderstanding of the key facts at the time the contract was made. If both a buyer and seller believed a painting was an original masterpiece but it turned out to be a forgery, and that belief was the entire reason the contract existed, rescission could apply.

Duress or Undue Influence — If someone was forced, threatened, or manipulated into signing an agreement, they did not give true free consent. Contracts entered under duress can be rescinded because genuine agreement never really existed.

Lack of Capacity — If a person was legally incapable of entering a contract at the time — for example, they were a minor, or mentally incapacitated — rescission can undo that agreement.

Failure of Consideration — "Consideration" in contract law means what each party gives in exchange (money, goods, services, a promise). If one party completely fails to deliver what they promised, the other party may be able to seek rescission.
Rescission vs. Termination: A Crucial Distinction

These two words are often confused, so it is worth making the difference crystal clear.

Termination ends a contract going forward from a certain point. Everything that happened before termination remains legally valid. If you hired someone for a year, paid them for six months, and then terminated the contract, those six months of payments and work stand — the contract just stops now.

Rescission goes further and says the contract was defective from birth. It is not just ended; it is annulled. It is as if it was never formed. The goal is to undo everything, returning all parties to their original positions. This is why courts take rescission very seriously — it is a much more powerful and complete remedy than simple termination.

A helpful way to remember this: termination is like closing a book at chapter six. Rescission is like shredding the book and pretending it was never written.
Two Types of Rescission

Mutual Rescission happens when both parties to a contract voluntarily and jointly agree to cancel it. They both want out. In this case, they simply agree that the contract is over and work out how to return things to the way they were. This is the most peaceful and straightforward form of rescission.

Unilateral Rescission is when only one party wants to cancel the contract, and they do so on legal grounds (such as fraud or misrepresentation). The other party may or may not agree. In these cases, the matter often ends up before a court, which then decides whether rescission is legally warranted.
Who Can Grant Rescission?

Rescission can be granted in two ways:

By agreement between the parties (mutual rescission, as described above), without needing a court.

By a court or legal authority, when one party applies for rescission and the court rules in their favor based on legal grounds like fraud or duress.
What Happens After Rescission?

Once rescission is granted or agreed upon, the legal doctrine of restitution kicks in. Restitution means restoring each party to their original position. Money is refunded. Property is returned. Any unjust enrichment — meaning any benefit one party unfairly gained from the other through the flawed contract — must be given back. The law tries to make it as though the contract simply never happened.
A Quick Real-World Example to Tie It All Together

You sign a contract to buy a piece of land for $50,000. You pay the money and the deal closes. Later, you discover that the seller had a legal obligation to tell you the land was contaminated, and they deliberately hid this from you — that is fraud.

You go to court and seek rescission of the contract. The court agrees. The contract is declared void from the very beginning. The seller must give you back your $50,000. You must give back the land. Neither party profits from the fraudulent deal. You are both, as closely as possible, returned to where you stood before any of it happened.

That entire process — the legal undoing of that contract from its root — is rescission.
In One Sentence
Rescission is the complete legal cancellation of a contract, law, or agreement that wipes it out as if it never existed, restoring all parties to their original position before it was made.
